newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: P-AND-O UNDER FIRE OVER TENDER
The Melbourne Port Authority says the tendering process it used for redevelopment of Appleton Dock is transparent and there's been no wrong doing.
P-and-O wants the Victorian Government to intervene, or face legal action, after losing its bid to Hong Kong based Orient Overseas Container Line, to develop and operate a new cargo facility.
Chief Executive Officer of Melbourne Port Corporation, Jeffrey Gilbert says he's disappointed that P-an-O should take what he calls a bully boy stance against the organisation.
The State Government has refused to intervene in the dispute.
HINDMARSH BRIDGE SAGA LUNACY: DEVELOPER
The woman who wants to develop South Australia's Hindmarsh Island says common sense has been thrown out the window, in the latest move on the bridge saga.
The Opposition and minor parties have blocked a Government Bill in the Senate, designed to prevent another inquiry into the proposed Hindmarsh Island Bridge.
They say the bill was unnecessary and would breach the Racial Discrimination Act.
Developer, Wendy Chapman, says Labor claims the Bridge must be built, but is sending the issue to another million-dollar inquiry and delaying it by at least another nine months.
She says the whole issue has reached the point of lunacy.
CHEAPER PAIN RELIEVERS JUST AS EFFECTIVE
The Australian Consumers Association says big savings can be made by ignoring marketing images for pain relievers.
The Association has studied 100 brands of pain relievers and found cheaper brands are just as effective as their more expensive competitors.
That's because many of the medications contain the same active ingredient.
The Association's Gail Kennedy says each two-tablet dose contained the same amount of active ingredient, yet the price of each dose ranged from six cents to 46 cents.
YOUTH APPEARS ON HANSON CHARGE
A seventeen-year-old-youth has appeared before the Ipswich Magistrates Court charged with using obscene language and obstructing police, after a confrontation with independent M-P Pauline Hanson.
She gave evidence against Paser Shefe saying he'd joined a group of youths in a heated debate with her, and that bad language had been used.
The obstruction charge was struck out because it was brought under a law repealed three years ago.
Mr Shefe was remanded on bail until May.
MINING ACCIDENT AT HUNTER VALLEY
In New South Wales, investigations are underway into another mining accident in the Hunter Valley.
Police say a 38-year old electrician from Neath was working with a gang on a coalface at the Munmorah colliary last night, when a section of the sandstone roof collapsed.
He was knocked to the ground, paramedics stablized him before he was airlifted to the John Hunter Hospital with arm and spinal injuries.
Police say the area that collapsed has been sealed-off.
An investigation has been launched by the Department of Mines and Energy.
DEMOCRATS SAYS SALE OF HOUSE FOR CARE WORTH CONSIDERING
The Australian Democrats say some older people should consider selling a home they no longer use, as way of paying for better care in nursing homes.

The Federal Government has announced details of the means-tested entry fee for nursing homes, and has again offered an assurance no-one will be forced to sell their home to gain entry to a nursing home.
But the Opposition claims older people who live alone, with their home as their only asset, will be forced to sell.
Democrats Family Services spokesman, John Woodley, says he doesn't want to see people on low incomes forced to sell their homes.
But he says some people should consider whether it's better to pay for a higher standard of nursing home care than continuing to own an empty house.
SCIENCE PRIZE WINNER SAYS HECS MOVE A CONCERN

One of the winners of this year's 300-thousand dollar Australia Prize for science, says Australia needs to develop a culture that encourages scientists to return home once they've gained experience overseas.
Professor Rodney Tucker has been recognised for playing a crucial role in the advent of the information superhighway.
Professor Tucker, along with another Australian and an Austrian scientist, will receive the award from the Prime Minister tonight.
The Professor says the day will come when homes will have access to such a vast communications network that phone calls will be offered free.
But he's also expressed concern about the Federal Government's decision to increase HECS charges for science courses.
He says measures are needed to build up research and development, and says it's important more people study science and engineering.
GILLIAN SHOULD INTENSIFY OVERNIGHT
The Weather Bureau in Queensland says tropical cyclone Gillian, off the north Queensland coast, should intensify into a category two cyclone overnight.
Cyclone Gillian is currently situated 500-kilometres east of Cooktown, and slowly moving southward.
Supervisor of the Cyclone Warning Centre, Jim Davidson, says Gillian poses a risk to communities between Cairns and Bowen.
Mr Davidson says the cyclone's expected to go from a category one of 990-hectapascals to at least a category two cyclone, overnight.
RAIL LINK TO BE CLOSED FOR ANOTHER TWO DAYS
Western Australia's coastal link to the North West will be closed for at least another two days, following flooding in the West Pilbara.
Main Roads says two 70-metre sections of the North West Coastal Highway have been destroyed by the swollen Ashburton River, south east of Onslow.
The road is expected to reopen on Wednesday morning.
Onslow remains isolated by road, and the town's airstrip is now also closed because of flooding.
The town is expected to be cut off for up to five days.
